newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan game maker targets multimedia for growth.
newsitem.headline: Japan game maker targets multimedia for growth.

text.p: Japanese game equipment maker Namco Ltd plans to use its computer graphics technology to expand into multimedia fields over the next decade.

"Ten years from now, 60 percent of our operations will still be video games, amusement arcades and theme parks. But the remaining 40 percent will be new enterprises," Namco president Masaya Nakamura said in a recent interview.
Namco has already begun testing the waters in film making using computer-aided technology.
Nakamura said the company aims to launch its first motion picture using computer graphics in the 1998 Christmas season in the United States.

The movie, which has an environmental theme, is currently being produced by a major computer graphics studio in Los Angeles and is expected to cost between four billion yen ($35.0 million) and five billion yen ($44 million).
The film will be shown first in the United States and then distributed in Japan.
The company will tap ailing movie-maker Nikkatsu Corp's vast network in Japan to distribute the movie, Nakamura said.
Namco announced last month it would take over financially troubled Nikkatsu, providing the firm with three billion yen ($26.3 million) in new capital at the end of this year.
Nakamura said Nikkatsu's large library of 5,000 films will help Namco develop its multimedia business.
However, Nikkatsu and its affiliate firms are estimated to have liabilities totalling 63 billion yen ($552 million), which will be a considerable burden for Namco.
Nakamura is also looking around for other troubled businesses.

He said the game maker has offered to provide management assistance to insolvent Phoenix Electric Co Ltd, which filed for reorganisation in November 1995 with group debt of about 19.5 billion yen ($171 million).
Nakamura said that Phoenix Electric, a maker of light bulbs and halogen lamps, has the potential to contribute to Namco's business development.
Namco expects to enjoy strong earnings results in the first half of the 1996/97 business year, buoyed by robust sales of game software for Sony Corp's 32-bit game machine PlayStation.
In September, Namco said it expected to post parent current profits of 4.5 billion yen ($39.4 million) in the April-September period, up from the previous forecast of 2.5 billion yen ($21.9 million).

Namco will hold off on introducing more software titles for Nintendo Co Ltd's 64-bit game machine, as demand for those machines was still not enough to create a profitable market for game software, Nakamura said.
Namco will also continue to actively expand its overseas business.
The company's revenues from exports has been steadily growing. The ratio of exports to total sales has risen from 5.16 percent in the 1991/92 business year to 12.25 percent in 1995/96.
"We hope to open more game arcades in shopping malls in the U.S. and cinema complexes in France," he said.
As of the end of September, Namco had 422 arcades and three theme parks in Japan. The company plans to expand into China and Europe before the end of this year.
Nakamura also said that Namco is considering expanding operations to Australia, Canada, Central and South America, and setting up a production base in Vietnam. ($1=114 yen)
